html:
The Servian Wall was a stone defensive wall built around the city of Rome in the early 4th century BCE. It was about 11 km long and up to 10 m high, with many gates, and it enclosed the seven hills.

The Romans named it after Servius Tullius, the sixth king of Rome, who was said to have walled the city in the 6th century BCE. There may have been earlier earth banks, but the stone wall is later. It was built soon after the Gauls sacked the city following the Battle of the Allia, from blocks of volcanic tuff quarried in the land of Veii, which Rome had just conquered.

The wall made Rome one of the hardest cities in Italy to take. When Hannibal marched up to the city in 211 BCE, he did not attack it. As Rome grew and ruled most of the Mediterranean, the wall stopped mattering, and buildings spread past it. In the 3rd century CE the emperor Aurelian built a new, much larger wall. Stretches of the Servian Wall still stand, the best known outside Termini railway station.
